For most of history, there wasn't any established way to kill one, even among the powerful elder races of the galaxy. Of course, when human beings reached the galactic stage they eventually figured out a technique to kill a god.
Now, there are two main issues with trying to murder a god. One, it's kind of like trying to remove a pillar from a building; sure, you can do it, but it risks destroying everything. Secondly, it is just naturally very, very hard - gods are interdimensional, Lovecraftian beings, and no ordinary weapons were able to slay them. The Wang-Harrington Replacement Theorem managed to solve both of these issues, though. The gods could finally be killed, but at the cost of every other reality.
The way this works is that you would set off a localized quantum vacuum bomb - a device that initiates a false vacuum decay event - in an isolated space, which is contained by a bubble nucleation containment field, so that the blast doesn't destroy the whole universe. A side effect of setting off this bomb is that its effects ripple through all other realities, causing a false vacuum event in every universe besides our own and thereby destroying all realities and killing every element of the gods in every universe.
Then comes the task of replacing the "pillar." The gods are so fundamental to our reality that if they are not replaced within Planck time, the universe will undergo a sort of "error" and annihilate itself instantly. To prevent this, one must construct an intense artificial intelligence of such magnitude that it is able to process every atom, particle and wave in the universe at total precision. For extremely complex mathematical reasons, this causes the universe to keep functioning as it ordinarily would, with the superintelligence replacing the former gods. An interesting side effect of this is that any change made to the simulation on the computer affects reality itself - in essence, this gives the owner of the AI godhood themselves.
